articles.title: Tatjana Smith: South African swimmer comes out of retirement
articles.summary: South Africa's most successful Olympian Tatjana Smith explains why she has reversed her decision to retire from competitive swimming.
articles.body:
Having ended a two-year exile from competitive swimming, South Africa's most successful Olympian Tatjana Smith has revealed she "lost the love" for her sport before stepping away from the pool in 2024.

The 29-year-old's decision to retire straight after the Paris Games came as a surprise, given she had just won 200m breaststroke gold in the French capital to add to her 100m title from Tokyo 2020.

But after two years away, which included several months in which she did not swim at all, Smith says she is now "free from the things that made me hate swimming".

"My whole life, I was kind of a robot towards swimming," she told Newsday on the BBC World Service.

"You're so zoned in, you're obsessed with something, so there isn't actually time for you to think about things outside of the pool that you potentially have a passion for.

"I think probably everyone would think that the timing [of retirement] was the worst. But I absolutely 100% believe it was the best decision at that time, and I still have so much peace about it."

Having also picked up a silver medal in both Tokyo and Paris, Smith's total of four Olympic medals for South Africa is matched only by fellow swimmer Chad le Clos, who claimed one gold and three silvers across the London 2012 and Rio 2016 Games.

Smith on retirement and becoming South Africa’s most decorated Olympian

But despite making history for her country, Smith says financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, also contributed to her decision to retire.

"The financial burden on any athlete is so tough," she explained.

"I relied on my parents funding me until I broke the world record at the Olympics. And then, all of a sudden, now people are interested in maybe sponsoring you.

"But the majority of sponsorships for athletes are based on performance. So then you have that pressure and expectation to always have to perform, otherwise you're not going to get paid.

"I think the financial side, and also being in a system where they're not really putting the athletes first, made it really difficult."

Smith won her first Olympic title under her maiden name Schoenmaker, before changing her surname when she married sports agent Joel Smith in 2023.

The marriage made her part of a wider South African sporting dynasty, given that her sister-in-law is Rachel Smith, who was married to Springboks captain Siya Kolisi before their split.

Tatjana Smith admits her own marriage changed the way she thought about her future.

"Thinking about families as a woman, you have to time it perfectly, because if you're pregnant, it's not like you can still compete."

While children are not yet part of her journey, Smith says working out what to do next was far from easy.

"I definitely understand what athletes mean from the post-Olympic depression," said the 2023 200m breaststroke world champion, who also counts Commonwealth and African titles among her achievements.

"It was such an emptiness in my life, because my whole life revolved around swimming.

"I don't have to eat at a certain time, I don't have to sleep at a certain time, I don't have to think about travelling or not spending time with family anymore.

"The world is so overwhelming. It's like, in which direction to go?

"It was definitely the toughest season that I had to go through. I think it's probably why it's made me a stronger person."

Initially, Smith took on speaking engagements to pay the bills.

She smiles when she admits: "I hate public speaking. I hate being in front of people."

The same cannot be said of her love for competition.

Having returned to the pool in order to keep fit, she decided to have a crack at triathlon, something she describes as a "crazy idea".

"The training was so intense, and I was like, 'OK, I might as well just go back to swimming if I'm going to train this hard'," she said.

"Every time I went back to the swimming pool and I dived in, I was like, 'Yeah, this is a feeling that I really miss so much'.

"I think slowly over the year and a half, I just realised 'Wow, I really do love swimming'."

Having made her decision to come out of retirement, Smith now wants to freshen things up and "try something new".

That means a change to the 50m breaststroke, an event which has just been added to the Olympic schedule for the first time ahead of the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.

"I thought, 'Why don't I try? Why don't I give myself that challenge? Reinvent myself'," said Smith.

"I always try and describe it to someone that maybe doesn't understand swimming; it's like a 400m runner and a 100m [runner]. It's two different body types, two different trainings, and that's where I'm going."

It means she has more than halved her training volume, with three sessions a week instead of eight - a change she believes will help her retain her love for her sport and live a more balanced life.

"I feel like I'm being so lazy because I used to do 12km per day and now the focus is on taking time to be as explosive as possible.

"I have 20 years of endurance in my pocket, but I can definitely see I don't have those fast twitch [muscle] fibres. It's a whole different way of teaching my body how to swim."

Those initial 20 years in the pool left Smith feeling burned out.

Now she says she has earned the right to do things on her terms.

"Swimming was an opportunity given to me by my parents and I believe I took it on full heartedly.

"But, for the first time, it's my decision whether I want to come back. I'm choosing swimming.

"I've achieved way more than I ever dreamed in my whole life, so I have nothing to prove."

articles.title: Where is the Village? PT Usha questions Asian Games accommodation model
articles.summary: Asian Games 2026 News: Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president P T Usha on Tuesday questioned the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games organisers' decision to do away with a conventi.
articles.body: Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president P T Usha on Tuesday questioned the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games organisers' decision to do away with a conventional Athletes Village, saying she and several other members of the event's coordination committee had objected to the plan.Usha, one of India's most successful Asian Games athletes, said an Athletes Village is about more than accommodation. She said it brings athletes from different countries together and creates the atmosphere that is associated with a multi-sport event.Athletes at the Aichi-Nagoya Games are being housed at different locations, with a cruise ship serving as the principal accommodation facility instead of a single purpose-built Village. The Games organisers have cited cost and sustainability as the main reasons for the arrangement, which has divided opinions."In fact, everybody objected. Most of the countries objected, actually...even I did," Usha said when asked about the decision not to build a traditional Games Village."I say that because I have travelled from 1982 until now and seen most of the villages. It is totally different from this, with the ship and everything. I think even the OCA (Olympic Council of Asia) did not want this, but somewhere or the other, they had to accept it," she added, as quoted by news gncy PTI.Asian Games full coverage | Schedule | Medal tallyUsha, who was part of the coordination committee, said the Village system had been defended because of the interaction it allows between athletes."I was a coordination committee member and most of the coordination team objected. We wanted the Village system because it is always good," she said."Everybody can come together, see each other and mix and mingle. That is what makes a Village so good."While saying that the accommodation itself was adequate, Usha said the lack of a centralised Village could lead to logistical and coordination challenges.She also pointed to the distance between venues as another issue with the way the Games have been organised.Having competed at multiple Asian Games, Olympics and Commonwealth Games, Usha said the venues at earlier editions were closer together, making it easier to watch different sports."The problem, for me, is that in our time, although we did not have many facilities, the venues were very close. If you wanted to go from one venue to another, it was very easy," she said."Here, if I have to go to shooting and then to cricket, I have to take another route. So I can only go to one venue if I want to see many Games."Usha acknowledged that the dispersed model could help different areas benefit from sporting infrastructure, but said it also made the venues less accessible."Maybe they (organisers) say that every place will have infrastructure and all, but this is the big difference I have felt," she said.Usha also rejected the suggestion that the arrangement in Japan could mark the end of the traditional Games Village."I don't think the Village culture will change because nobody, when we were in the committee, liked this idea," she said.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: European Athletics Championships to have £3m record prize fund in 2028
articles.summary: The European Athletics Championships will have a total record prize fund worth £3m when it takes place in Poland in 2028.
articles.body:
The European Athletics Championships in 2028 will offer a record prize fund worth about £3m when they are staged in Silesia, Poland.

Prize money will be awarded to athletes finishing in the top eight across all 50 events.

Gold medal winners will earn 30,000 euros (£25,720), while silver and bronze medallists will receive 15,000 euros (£12,860) and 10,000 euros (£8,573) respectively.

Athletes finishing fourth to eighth across the 50 disciplines will receive awards of 5,000, 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 euros respectively.

European Athletics has restructured the way in which prize money is awarded, ensuring athletes finishing in the top eight in every discipline receive financial recognition.

The prize fund on offer at the last championships, held in Birmingham in August of this year, did not involve a standard payout for every medal position.

Instead, a total pot of 500,000 euros (£428,000) was split equally between the top 10 performances across 10 categories - five for men and five for women - determined by the World Athletics scoring tables.

Great Britain and Northern Ireland won 19 medals in Birmingham, including nine golds.

But none of those gold medal performances earned one of the 50,000 euro 'Gold Crown' bonuses awarded by the organisers.

The significant increase in money for the European Championships reflects how elite athletes' on-track earning potential is growing.

World Athletics recently provided what it described as "the richest prize pot in the history of the sport", with $10m (£7.4m) put up for its new three-day Ultimate Championship event in Budapest.

Each individual event winner received $150,000 (£110,000).

How did the first Ultimate Championship go?

How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage

With athletes carefully planning their seasons, championships may need to offer substantial incentives to ensure strong fields.

There will be another Ultimate Championship in 2028, plus the Los Angeles Olympics and a Diamond League season.

The European Championships will take place in early June, starting six weeks before the Olympics get under way.

European Athletics said its revised structure for 2028 ensures every discipline is treated equally and there will now be "due recognition" given not only to medal winners but to all athletes reaching the top eight.

The governing body's chief executive, Christian Milz, said the decision "demonstrates our commitment" to competitors who are "at the heart of our sport".

"We are seeing European athletes produce extraordinary performances and capture the imagination of audiences around the world," he said.

"It is important that we continue to find meaningful ways to recognise and support them, and this record prize fund is a significant step in that direction."
